CHAPTER 2.4 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.4 · LEARNING AREA 2 · JANUARY

Families, functions from conditions and optimisation

Now you turn curve sketching round and put it to use: you investigate whole families of functions with a parameter, build a function from a profile of conditions and find the best box, the most economical can and the largest enclosure. Optimisation problems are the high point of differential calculus, and they appear in almost every exam.

7 LESSONS3 UNITSCLASS TEST 2SUSTAINABILITY
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate points of intersection and points of contact of two graphs
  • investigate families of functions with a case analysis and find loci
  • set up equations of functions from conditions and solve the system of equations with the graphing calculator
  • solve optimisation problems: objective function, constraint, domain, values at the ends

UNIT 12.5 LESSONS

1Points of intersection and contact, families of functions

$x^2 = 2x - 1$ leads to $(x - 1)^2 = 0$: only one, double solution $x = 1$. At the point $(1, 1)$ both graphs also have the same gradient, $f'(1) = 2$. The line touches the parabola; it is its tangent.

You find common points of two graphs by setting them equal. At a point of contact the gradients agree as well. A family of functions $f_a$ contains a parameter $a$. You calculate with $a$ as with a fixed number and often have to distinguish at the end which case occurs for which $a$.

KEY POINT · TOUCHING AND FAMILIES

Points of intersection: solve $f(x) = g(x)$ · point of contact at $x_0$: $f(x_0) = g(x_0)$ and $f'(x_0) = g'(x_0)$

Family: for every $a$ you get a function $f_a$. Find properties depending on $a$, distinguish cases such as $a > 0$, $a = 0$, $a < 0$.

Locus of the turning points: solve $x_E$ for $a$ and substitute into $y_E$.

Double solution: if $f(x) - g(x) = 0$ has a double zero, the graphs touch there.

On the graphing calculator: draw several curves of the family with a list, for example $a = \{1, 2, 3\}$.

INTERACTIVE · A FAMILY OF FUNCTIONS

Move the parameter $a$. The turning points of all the curves of the family lie on one common curve, the locus.

EXAMPLE 1 · POINTS OF INTERSECTION

Calculate the points of intersection of $f(x) = x^3 - x$ and $g(x) = 3x$.

$x^3 - 4x = 0$, $x(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0$.

$(0, 0)$, $(2, 6)$, $(-2, -6)$

EXAMPLE 2 · A FAMILY WITH A CASE ANALYSIS

Investigate $f_a(x) = x^3 - ax$ for turning points and find their locus.

$f_a'(x) = 3x^2 - a$. For $a > 0$: $x = \pm\sqrt{a/3}$, a maximum and a minimum. For $a = 0$: a saddle point. For $a < 0$: no turning points.

From $a = 3x^2$ it follows that $y = x^3 - 3x^2 \cdot x$: locus $y = -2x^3$. For $a = 3$: $H(-1, 2)$, $T(1, -2)$.

EXERCISES

Calculate the points of intersection of $f(x) = x^2 - 2$ and $g(x) = x$.

$x^2 - x - 2 = 0$: $(2, 2)$ and $(-1, -1)$

Show that $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = 2x$ touch.

$x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2 = 0$, and $f'(1) = 2 = g'(1)$: point of contact $(1, 2)$.

Find the vertex of $f_a(x) = -x^2 + ax$ depending on $a$. For which $a$ is it at $(2, 4)$? On which curve do all the vertices lie?

$f_a'(x) = -2x + a = 0$: $S\left(\tfrac{a}{2}, \tfrac{a^2}{4}\right)$. $a = 4$ gives $(2, 4)$. With $x = \tfrac{a}{2}$, $y = x^2$: the standard parabola.

For which $a$ does $f_a(x) = x^2 + ax + 4$ have two zeros, one zero or none?

Discriminant $\tfrac{a^2}{4} - 4$: two for $|a| > 4$, one for $a = \pm 4$, none for $|a| < 4$.

For which $a$ does the line through the origin $y = ax$ touch the parabola $f(x) = x^2 + 1$? Give the points of contact.

$x^2 - ax + 1 = 0$ is to have exactly one solution.

$\tfrac{a^2}{4} - 1 = 0$: $a = \pm 2$, points of contact $(1, 2)$ and $(-1, 2)$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the positive $x$-coordinate of a point of intersection of $x^3 - x$ and $3x$?

$x^3 - 4x = 0$

What is the $y$-coordinate of the maximum of $f_3(x) = x^3 - 3x$?

$H(-1, 2)$

Two graphs touch at $x_0$ if …

Both have to be true.

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Equations of functions from conditions

The arch is a parabola $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$. At the origin: $f(0) = 0$, so $c = 0$. Maximum at $(2, 4)$: $f(2) = 4a + 2b = 4$ and $f'(2) = 4a + b = 0$. Subtracting gives $b = 4$, then $a = -1$. The arch is $f(x) = -x^2 + 4x$.

In a “function from conditions” problem the graph is described and you are looking for the equation. You choose an approach with general coefficients, translate every property into an equation and solve the system of linear equations. A function of degree $n$ has $n + 1$ coefficients, so you need $n + 1$ conditions.

KEY POINT · TRANSLATING CONDITIONS

Point $P(u, v)$ on the graph: $f(u) = v$ · gradient $m$ at $x_0$: $f'(x_0) = m$

Turning point at $x_E$: $f'(x_E) = 0$ · point of inflection at $x_W$: $f''(x_W) = 0$ · horizontal inflectional tangent: also $f'(x_W) = 0$

Symmetric about the $y$-axis: only even exponents in the approach · about the origin: only odd

At the end, a check: does the function really satisfy all the conditions, is the turning point really one?

With the graphing calculator: enter the coefficients as a matrix and let it solve with rref (reduced row echelon form), or use the equation solver.

Symmetry saves work: a quartic approach symmetric about the $y$-axis, $ax^4 + bx^2 + c$, has only three unknowns.

INTERACTIVE · THE PROFILE

Choose the type of conditions and drag the points. The widget sets up the system of equations and solves it; the curve follows at once.

EXAMPLE 3 · USING SYMMETRY

A cubic function is point-symmetric about the origin and has the minimum $T(1, -2)$. Find its equation.

Approach $f(x) = ax^3 + bx$. $f(1) = a + b = -2$ and $f'(1) = 3a + b = 0$: $a = 1$, $b = -3$.

$f(x) = x^3 - 3x$. Check: $f''(1) = 6 > 0$, so it really is a minimum.

EXAMPLE 4 · SADDLE POINT

The graph of a cubic function passes through the origin and has a point of inflection with a horizontal tangent at $W(1, 1)$.

$d = 0$, $f(1) = a + b + c = 1$, $f'(1) = 3a + 2b + c = 0$, $f''(1) = 6a + 2b = 0$.

Solution $a = 1$, $b = -3$, $c = 3$: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x$

EXERCISES

Find the parabola through $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(2, 3)$.

$c = 1$, $a + b = -1$, $4a + 2b = 2$: $a = 2$, $b = -3$, so $f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1$.

Translate into equations: a) The graph has the gradient 3 at $P(2, 5)$.   b) There is a point of inflection at $x = 1$.   c) It cuts the $y$-axis at 4.

a) $f(2) = 5$ and $f'(2) = 3$   b) $f''(1) = 0$   c) $f(0) = 4$

A quartic function symmetric about the $y$-axis has the maximum $(0, 4)$ and minima at $(\pm 2, 0)$. Find it.

$f(x) = ax^4 + bx^2 + c$: $c = 4$, $16a + 4b + 4 = 0$, $32a + 4b = 0$: $a = \tfrac14$, $b = -2$. $f(x) = 0.25x^4 - 2x^2 + 4 = 0.25(x^2 - 4)^2$

A cubic function passes through the origin, has the minimum $T(2, -4)$ and a point of inflection at $x = 1$. Compare with exercise 15 from chapter 2.3.

$d = 0$, $8a + 4b + 2c = -4$, $12a + 4b + c = 0$, $6a + 2b = 0$: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2$, exactly the function from chapter 2.3.

A path is to lead without a kink from the level $y = 0$ (for $x \le 0$) to the level $y = 2$ (for $x \ge 4$). Find the cubic function for the transition piece. How steep is it at its steepest point?

Without a kink means: at the joins the height and the gradient agree, $f'(0) = f'(4) = 0$.

$f(0) = 0$, $f'(0) = 0$, $f(4) = 2$, $f'(4) = 0$: $f(x) = -\tfrac{1}{16}x^3 + \tfrac38 x^2$. The steepest point is at the point of inflection at $x = 2$: $f'(2) = 0.75$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Point-symmetric, cubic, minimum $T(1, -2)$: what is $a$ in $ax^3 + bx$?

$a = 1$, $b = -3$

The parabola through $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$, $(2, 3)$: what is $a$?

$2x^2 - 3x + 1$

How many conditions do you need for a cubic function without symmetry?

four coefficients $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$

UNIT 32.5 LESSONS

3Optimisation problems: objective function and constraint

The box made from 30 cm × 20 cm with the edge $x$ has the volume $V(x) = x(30 - 2x)(20 - 2x)$ for $0 < x < 10$. $V'(x) = 12x^2 - 200x + 600 = 0$ gives $x \approx 3.92$ cm; the other solution lies outside. The best box holds about 1056.3 cm³, only a little more than the one with $x = 4$ cm (1056 cm³).

In an optimisation problem a quantity is to be as large or as small as possible. Usually it depends at first on two variables that are linked by a constraint. With it you eliminate one variable and get the objective function in one variable, which you investigate as in chapter 2.3.

KEY POINT · STEPS TO A SOLUTION

1. Make a sketch, name the quantities · 2. Main condition: formula for the quantity to be optimised · 3. Solve the constraint for one variable and substitute: objective function

4. Fix the domain · 5. Extremum: $f' = 0$ and the sufficient condition · 6. Check the values at the ends · 7. Answer in a sentence with units

Sustainability: the optimal can needs the least tin for the same volume. With millions of cans that saves tonnes of material.

With the graphing calculator: draw the objective function and let it calculate the maximum in the domain. Don’t forget the ends.

INTERACTIVE · OPTIMISING

Choose a problem and move the variable. The graph of the objective function shows where the optimum is. First try it out, then calculate with $f' = 0$.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE ENCLOSURE AGAINST THE WALL

With 60 m of fencing, a rectangular enclosure is to be marked out against a wall. What is the largest possible area?

Two sides $x$ at right angles to the wall, one side $y$ parallel to it: $2x + y = 60$. $A(x) = x(60 - 2x)$ for $0 < x < 30$.

$A'(x) = 60 - 4x = 0$: $x = 15$, $y = 30$, $A = 450$ m². $A'' = -4 < 0$: maximum.

EXAMPLE 6 · THE ECONOMICAL CAN

A cylindrical can is to hold one litre. For which radius do you need the least tin?

Constraint $\pi r^2 h = 1000$, so $h = \tfrac{1000}{\pi r^2}$. Objective function $S(r) = 2\pi r^2 + \tfrac{2000}{r}$.

$S'(r) = 4\pi r - \tfrac{2000}{r^2} = 0$: $r^3 = \tfrac{500}{\pi}$, $r \approx 5.42$ cm, $h \approx 10.84$ cm. The height is exactly the diameter.

EXERCISES

Two numbers have the sum 20. When is their product largest?

$P(x) = x(20 - x)$, $P'(x) = 20 - 2x = 0$: both 10, product 100.

Which rectangle with the perimeter 40 cm has the largest area?

$A(a) = a(20 - a)$, maximum at $a = 10$: the square with 100 cm².

Under the parabola $f(x) = 9 - x^2$ there is a rectangle with two vertices on the $x$-axis and two vertices on the parabola. What is its largest possible area?

Vertex $(u, 9 - u^2)$: $A(u) = 2u(9 - u^2)$, $A'(u) = 18 - 6u^2 = 0$, $u = \sqrt3$. $A = 12\sqrt3 \approx 20.78$.

A box open at the top with a square base is to hold 500 cm³. For which dimensions do you need the least material?

$x^2 h = 500$, $S(x) = x^2 + 4xh = x^2 + \tfrac{2000}{x}$, $S'(x) = 2x - \tfrac{2000}{x^2} = 0$: $x = 10$ cm, $h = 5$ cm, $S = 300$ cm².

Which points of the standard parabola are closest to the point $P(0, 3)$?

Optimise the square of the distance; it has its minimum at the same point: $d^2(x) = x^2 + (x^2 - 3)^2$.

$d^2 = x^4 - 5x^2 + 9$, derivative $4x^3 - 10x = 0$: $x = 0$ (local maximum, distance 3) or $x^2 = 2.5$. $(\pm 1.58, 2.5)$ with the distance $\sqrt{2.75} \approx 1.66$.

TEST YOURSELF!

60 m of fencing against a wall: what is the largest possible area of the enclosure?

$15 \cdot 30$

What is the radius of the most economical one-litre can, to two decimal places?

$r = \sqrt[3]{500/\pi}$

Open box, square base, 500 cm³: how long is the base edge?

$x^3 = 1000$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

For which $a$ does $f_a(x) = x^2 - 2ax + 1$ have a double zero?

Discriminant $a^2 - 1 = 0$: $a = \pm 1$

Connecting with Year 11: find the parabola through $(-1, 6)$, $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$ with the elimination method.

Subtract the first two equations: $2b = -4$, $b = -2$. Then $a + c = 4$ and $4a + c = 7$: $a = 1$, $c = 3$, so $f(x) = x^2 - 2x + 3$.

A rectangle has the diagonal 10 cm. When is its area largest?

$b = \sqrt{100 - a^2}$, maximum of $A^2 = a^2(100 - a^2)$ at $a^2 = 50$: the square with $a \approx 7.07$ cm and $A = 50$ cm².

A window consists of a rectangle with a semicircle on top. Its perimeter is 6 m. For which radius does the most light come in?

$2h + 2r + \pi r = 6$, $A(r) = 2rh + \tfrac{\pi}{2} r^2 = 6r - \left(2 + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) r^2$. $A'(r) = 0$: $r = \tfrac{6}{4 + \pi} \approx 0.84$ m. Then $h \approx 0.84$ m as well, and the area is about 2.52 m².

EXCURSIONNATURE

Why honeycombs are hexagonal

Bees build their combs from wax, and wax is expensive: for one gram they need a lot of honey. So the walls should be as short as possible, but the cells the same size. Only three regular polygons fill the plane without gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. For a cell with area 1 the perimeter is about 4.56 for the triangle, 4 for the square and only 3.72 for the hexagon.

The hexagonal shape of honeycombs was already admired in antiquity. The honeycomb conjecture goes further: among all ways of dividing the plane into cells of equal size, the hexagonal grid has the shortest walls, even compared with curved shapes. It was only proved by Thomas Hales in 1999, an optimisation problem for which you need more than the derivative.

Source: T. C. Hales, “The Honeycomb Conjecture”, Discrete & Computational Geometry 25 (2001), pp. 1–22; preprint arXiv:math/9906042 (1999).
